title: Sustainable Agriculture and Biotechnology Concerns

cards.b:
The Green Revolution fed India but drained groundwater, loaded soils with chemicals and cut diversity. Natural farming and GM crops are both in the news, and UPSC asks for balanced views.

This lesson covers the farm-side answer and the biotech debate.

It aims to produce enough food while protecting soil, water and biodiversity and keeping farmers’ incomes stable. Methods: organic farming, integrated pest management, crop rotation, conservation agriculture, drip irrigation, agroforestry, System of Rice Intensification.

Related ideas: agroecology, climate-smart agriculture and regenerative practices.

Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (2015) promotes organic clusters. Sikkim became India’s first fully organic state in 2016. The National Mission on Natural Farming (approved November 2024) aims to bring around a crore farmers into chemical-free farming.

Soil Health Card (2015), neem-coated urea and PM-PRANAM (2023, to cut chemical fertiliser) support the shift. PMKSY promotes “per drop more crop.”

The UN observed 2023 as the International Year of Millets at India’s initiative. Millets are hardy and need little water, so they suit dry areas. Micro-irrigation saves water and fertiliser.

Debate: can organic farming feed India? Sri Lanka’s abrupt 2021 chemical ban, which hurt yields, is often cited as a warning against sudden shifts.

Bt cotton (approved 2002) is the only GM crop in commercial cultivation in India. The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) under the Environment Protection Act (Rules 1989) approves GM releases.

Bt brinjal was put under a moratorium in 2010 by Environment Minister Jairam Ramesh. GM mustard (DMH-11) was cleared by GEAC in October 2022; the Supreme Court gave a split verdict in July 2024 and asked the Centre to frame a national GM policy.

In 2022 the Centre exempted certain genome-edited plants (SDN-1 and SDN-2) without foreign DNA from GM rules. In May 2025, India released two genome-edited rice varieties developed by ICAR institutes.

Supporters say this is faster and safer than transgenics. Critics seek tight oversight and labelling.

• Gene flow to wild relatives and loss of crop diversity.
  • Pest resistance (pink bollworm in Bt cotton).
  • Corporate control of seeds and high prices; fears over terminator seeds (GURTs), which are not allowed.
  • Health and allergen questions; labelling.
  • Unapproved herbicide-tolerant cotton spreading illegally.

The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act 2001 protects breeders and farmers’ right to save and sell seeds. The Biological Diversity Act 2002 controls access to biological resources and fights biopiracy (cases: neem, turmeric, basmati). The Cartagena Protocol (2000) governs biosafety of GMOs.

Geographical Indications protect traditional products.

Biotech can raise yields, cut pesticide use and add nutrition (golden rice, biofortified crops). Risks include corporate dominance and unknown long-term effects. Many experts want case-by-case approval, independent testing and public data.

A sustainable path can use both: agroecology as the base and tested biotech as a tool.

Mains-style: “GM crops: a boon or a bane for Indian agriculture? Discuss.” Structure: status (Bt cotton only); benefits; concerns; regulation (GEAC, Cartagena); court position (GM mustard 2024); way forward (transparent science, gene-editing rules, farmer choice).

Mains-style: “How can natural farming help achieve sustainable agriculture in India?”

Prelims tip: Bt cotton 2002; Bt brinjal moratorium 2010; GEAC under EPA; Sikkim organic 2016; Cartagena = biosafety.

quiz.w: It was adopted in 2000 under the CBD.

quiz.q: Which Act protects farmers’ rights over seeds?
quiz.w: It balances breeders’ and farmers’ rights.
